title: The Last First: Grace, Greatness, and a Ransom
summary: Jesus tells of a landowner who hires workers through the day and pays those who worked one hour the same denarius as those who worked twelve, and he defends his generosity against their grumbling. On the road to Jerusalem he predicts his death a third time, now naming crucifixion. When the mother of James and John asks for the places at his right and left, Jesus teaches that greatness in his kingdom is service, as the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve and to give his life as a ransom for many. Leaving Jericho, he has compassion on two blind men, touches their eyes, and they see and follow him.
story:
The chapter continues the conversation that closed chapter 19. Peter had asked what the disciples would receive for leaving everything (19:27), and Jesus had promised thrones and a hundredfold before warning that many first will be last (19:30). The parable of the vineyard, found only in Matthew, answers Peter's question from another side: the kingdom's rewards are given by the owner's generosity, not calculated by hours served, and those who count will be offended by grace. The same saying about the last and the first closes the parable (20:16), so the story is framed as a commentary on it.

The disciples still do not grasp it. Immediately after the third and most detailed prediction of the passion, the mother of two of the three closest disciples asks for the highest seats. Jesus' reply gathers the teaching of this whole section of Matthew, which began when he first spoke of the cross (16:21), into one sentence about the Son of Man who came to serve and to give his life as a ransom. The chapter ends at Jericho, the last town before the climb to Jerusalem, with two blind men who ask not for seats but for sight, and who follow him. The next chapter begins the entry into the city.
historical:
Galilean pilgrims going up to Jerusalem for Passover either crossed Samaria, as Josephus says was their custom (Antiquities 20.118), or went down the Jordan valley on its eastern side and crossed near Jericho, as Jesus does. Jericho in Jesus' day was a prosperous oasis about 250 meters (825 feet) below sea level, famous for its date palms and balsam groves. Herod the Great built winter palaces there, excavated at Tulul Abu el-Alayiq by Ehud Netzer from the 1970s, and he died there, probably in 4 BC. The Herodian town lay about 2 kilometers south of the mound of Old Testament Jericho, and from it a steep road of about 25 kilometers (15 miles) climbed roughly a thousand meters to Jerusalem, which is why the Gospels speak of going ‘up’ (verses 17 and 18). The crowd that followed Jesus out of Jericho (verse 29) was probably swelled by pilgrims going up for the feast.

The parable reflects the economy of Roman Palestine. Much of the best land belonged to large estates, and many villagers had lost their holdings through debt and taxation and hired themselves out by the day, especially at harvest, when grapes had to be picked and pressed before they spoiled. A denarius, a silver coin bearing the emperor's image (22:19-21), was a normal day's pay for such work. Tacitus reports that in AD 14 the legions on the Rhine, who were paid ten asses a day, mutinied and demanded a full denarius (Annals 1.17), which shows that a denarius a day was regarded as a decent wage for a laborer. The law of Moses required employers to pay hired workers before sunset, since they lived on each day's wage (Leviticus 19:13, Deuteronomy 24:14-15), and the Mishnah works out the rule for day and night laborers (m. Bava Metzia 9:11-12).

The third passion prediction (verses 18 and 19) is the only one of the three in Matthew to name crucifixion, and it adds that the Son of Man will be handed over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged. Crucifixion was a Roman penalty, used chiefly for slaves, rebels, and provincials, and in Judea only the Roman governor could order it; the Jewish council probably could not carry out a death sentence on its own under Roman rule (compare John 18:31). The prediction therefore foresees what chapters 26 and 27 narrate: a condemnation by the chief priests and scribes, and an execution by Pilate's soldiers.

James and John were the sons of Zebedee, Galilean fishermen called with their father's boat (4:21-22). Their mother appears again at the cross among the women who had followed Jesus from Galilee (27:56). Some interpreters, comparing Mark 15:40 and John 19:25, have identified her as Salome and as the sister of Jesus' mother, which would make James and John Jesus' cousins, but both identifications are uncertain. Jesus' word that they would drink his cup (verse 23) was fulfilled for James when Herod Agrippa I had him executed with the sword, around AD 44 (Acts 12:2), the first of the Twelve to die for his faith. Of John, Irenaeus reports that he lived at Ephesus into the reign of Trajan (Against Heresies 3.3.4, 2.22.5), while the fifth-century historian Philip of Side and the ninth-century chronicler George the Monk claim that Papias said John was killed by the Jews; most historians doubt the report or think it confused.

The rulers of the Gentiles who ‘lord it over them’ (verse 25) were a daily reality. Rome governed Judea through prefects and client kings, and Herod's son Archelaus had ruled so brutally that Augustus deposed him in AD 6 (Josephus, Antiquities 17.342-344). Matthew, as he does elsewhere (8:28), reports two healed men where Mark 10:46-52 names one, Bartimaeus; Luke 18:35-43 places the healing as Jesus approaches Jericho rather than as he leaves it.
cultural:
Day laborers gathered in the marketplace at dawn to be hired, and those left standing in the late afternoon were the ones no one wanted: the old, the weak, the known troublemakers. They were in some ways worse off than slaves, who at least were fed by their masters. A day without work could mean a family without bread. The hours are counted from sunrise, so the third hour is about nine in the morning, the sixth noon, the ninth about three, and the eleventh about five, an hour before the end of the working day. The first workers agree to a denarius; the later ones are promised ‘whatever is right’ (verse 4), and the last are simply sent. The foreman (epitropos, a steward or manager) pays at evening, as the law required.

The owner's reply to the grumblers uses three familiar expressions. He calls the spokesman ‘Friend’ (hetaire), a polite but distant address that in Matthew is always spoken to someone in the wrong: the guest without a wedding garment (22:12) and Judas at his arrest (26:50). He asks whether he may not do as he wishes with what is his, the right of an owner. And he asks, literally, ‘Is your eye evil because I am good?’ (verse 15). The ‘evil eye’ in Jewish idiom meant envy and stinginess, the grudging look at another's good or a begrudged gift (Deuteronomy 15:9, Proverbs 23:6, 28:22, Sirach 14:8-10); its opposite, the ‘good eye’, meant generosity. The Mishnah records that when Yohanan ben Zakkai asked his disciples for the good way a person should cling to, Rabbi Eliezer answered ‘a good eye’, and for the evil way to avoid, ‘an evil eye’ (m. Avot 2:9), and it classes a person who wants to give but begrudges others' giving as having an evil eye (m. Avot 5:13).

The mother's request follows the customs of a royal court. She comes kneeling (proskynousa, verse 20), the posture of a petitioner before a king, and asks Jesus to ‘declare’ it, as a king's word settles an appointment. The places at the right and left of a king were the highest honor and authority: Bathsheba sat at Solomon's right hand (1 Kings 2:19), and Psalm 110:1 seats the LORD's king at his right hand. In the Old Testament the cup is a common image for the portion God pours out, often the cup of his wrath (Psalm 75:8, Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15).

In verses 26 to 28 Jesus uses the vocabulary of the household. A diakonos was a servant who waited at table; a doulos was a slave, the lowest person in the house, owned and without rights. A ransom (lutron) was the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner of war, or the payment by which a life forfeited under the law could be redeemed (Exodus 21:30, Numbers 3:46-49). Blind people in the ancient world were usually reduced to begging, and the road out of Jericho, busy with pilgrims before Passover, was a good place to beg. ‘Son of David’ named the royal Messiah promised to David (2 Samuel 7:12-16), and Jewish tradition also remembered David's son Solomon as a healer with power over demons (Josephus, Antiquities 8.45-49), which may be why the title is so often joined to healing in Matthew (9:27, 12:23, 15:22).
literary:
The parable of the vineyard workers (verses 1 to 16) is built in two movements, the hiring (verses 1 to 7) and the payment (verses 8 to 15), followed by the saying that frames it (verse 16, reversing 19:30). The hiring scenes repeat with variation: the owner goes out at dawn, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, and at the eleventh, and the dialogue grows as the day goes on, until the last workers explain that no one has hired them. The payment scene depends on the order: by paying the last first, the owner makes sure the first see what the last receive, and the reader, like the first workers, expects a sliding scale. The story ends not with the workers' answer but with the owner's three questions, the last of which, ‘are you envious because I am generous?’, is left hanging for the hearer.

The chapter then sets side by side the third prediction of the passion (verses 17 to 19) and the request for honor (verses 20 to 28), the pattern Matthew has followed since 16:21: each time Jesus speaks of his death, the disciples misunderstand, and he teaches what following him costs. Matthew's form of the request differs from Mark's. In Mark 10:35 James and John ask for themselves; in Matthew their mother makes the request, but Jesus answers the sons in the plural (‘You do not know what you are asking’), and the brothers answer ‘We can’. Matthew omits Mark's saying about baptism and keeps the cup. The ten's indignation shows that they wanted the same thing, and Jesus' reply moves from a contrast (the rulers of the Gentiles) to a command (whoever wants to be great must be a servant) to its ground in his own mission (the Son of Man came to serve).

The healing at Jericho (verses 29 to 34) closes the section. Matthew shortens Mark's account, leaving out Bartimaeus's name and his thrown-off cloak, and he adds two touches of his own: Jesus is ‘moved with compassion’ and touches their eyes. He also doubles the figure, as he did with the demoniacs (8:28), and the scene closely resembles an earlier healing of two blind men who cried ‘Son of David, have mercy on us’ (9:27-31). Matthew frames the second half of the chapter with a question. Jesus asks the mother ‘What do you want?’ (verse 21) and the blind men ‘What do you want Me to do for you?’ (verse 32). One asks for thrones, the others for sight, and the chapter's last word is that they followed him.

outline.t: The parable of the workers in the vineyard
The third prediction of death and resurrection
The request of Zebedee's sons: greatness as service
Two blind men receive sight at Jericho

doctrines.note: Verse 28 is one of the Gospels' clearest statements of the meaning of Jesus' death: the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many, a price paid to set others free, given ‘in place of’ them (anti). The words echo Isaiah 53:10-12, where the servant's life is made a guilt offering and he bears the sin of many, and Matthew's Last Supper repeats the ‘many’ (26:28). Christians have developed the image in more than one way, as liberation from sin and evil powers and as Christ bearing what others owed, but the verse stresses that his death is a costly act of service in the place of others.

The landowner's generosity pictures God's grace. Those who come late receive the same gift as those who came early, because the gift depends on the giver's goodness, not on the worker's hours. The complaint of the first workers shows how grace offends those who think of God's kingdom as a system of wages.

Jesus forbids his followers to exercise authority as Gentile rulers do. In his community whoever wants to be great must be a servant and whoever wants to be first must be a slave, and he grounds this not in a technique of management but in his own death. Service is the shape of every office among his people.

The kingdom of heaven is like an owner who is generous to the last (verse 1), and its places of honor are assigned by the Father, not won by request (verse 23). It reverses human rank, so that the last are first, and it is entered by those who, like the blind men, ask for mercy.

The blind men call Jesus ‘Lord, Son of David’, and he acts as David's heir by showing mercy, just before he enters David's city. His messiahship is defined in this chapter by the cross: the one who will reign gives his life, and the places at his right and left will be seen at his crucifixion (27:38).

words.note: Dēnarion, denarius, a Roman silver coin. It occurs sixteen times in the New Testament, four in this parable. It was the ordinary pay for a day's labor and bore the emperor's image (22:19-21). Every worker in the parable receives exactly one: the first because it was agreed, the last because the owner chose to give it. The equal payment is the parable's scandal and its point.

Ponēros, evil, bad, wicked. It occurs about seventy-eight times in the New Testament and twenty-six times in Matthew, which uses it for the evil one (6:13, 13:19) and for an evil generation (12:39). In verse 15 it forms the idiom of the ‘evil eye’, the envious and grudging look, set against the owner's being ‘good’ (agathos). The same contrast appears in 6:22-23, where a healthy eye fills the body with light and an evil eye with darkness.

Potērion, cup. It occurs about thirty-one times in the New Testament and seven times in Matthew: a cup of cold water (10:42), the cup of this chapter (verses 22 and 23), the cup of the Last Supper, which is his blood of the covenant poured out for many (26:27-28), and the cup of Gethsemane, which he asks might pass from him (26:39, 42). In the prophets the cup is often the portion of God's wrath (Isaiah 51:17, Jeremiah 25:15), and Jesus takes it as a name for his suffering, which the brothers will share in their own way.

Katakurieuō, to lord it over, to exercise dominion over. It occurs four times in the New Testament: here, the parallel Mark 10:42, Acts 19:16 (an evil spirit overpowering the sons of Sceva), and 1 Peter 5:3, where elders are told not to lord it over those entrusted to them. The prefix kata gives the sense of domination bearing down on others. Jesus pairs it with katexousiazō, to exercise authority over, to describe power used for the ruler's own benefit.

Diakoneō, to serve, originally to wait at table. It occurs thirty-seven times in the New Testament and six times in Matthew, where angels serve Jesus (4:11), Peter's mother-in-law serves (8:15), the women from Galilee served him (27:55), and here, twice, the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve (verse 28). The related noun diakonos, servant, in verse 26, later named an office in the church (Philippians 1:1). In Daniel 7:14 all peoples serve the one like a son of man; Jesus reverses the picture.

Lutron, ransom, the price of release. It occurs only here and in the parallel Mark 10:45, though related words are common (antilutron in 1 Timothy 2:6, lutroō in Titus 2:14 and 1 Peter 1:18). In the Greek Old Testament it names the payment that redeems a firstborn or a forfeited life (Exodus 21:30, Numbers 3:46-49) and the redemption price of land and slaves (Leviticus 25:24, 51). BDAG gives the sense price of release. Joined with anti, ‘in place of’, it describes Jesus' life given for others. The text does not say to whom the ransom is paid, a question theologians have debated since the third century.

Splanchnizomai, to be moved with compassion, from splanchna, the inward parts thought to be the seat of feeling. It occurs twelve times in the New Testament, all in the first three Gospels, always of Jesus or of a figure in his parables who stands for God (the master in 18:27, the father in Luke 15:20, the Samaritan in Luke 10:33). Matthew adds it here to Mark's account (verse 34), as he does of Jesus' response to the crowds (9:36, 14:14, 15:32). The one who has just spoken of giving his life is moved to the core by two beggars.

christ:
The chapter's summit is Jesus' description of his own mission in verse 28. The Son of Man is the figure of Daniel 7:13-14, to whom all peoples, nations, and languages were to give service. Jesus reverses the picture: he came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many. The phrase gathers the language of Isaiah's servant, who pours out his life to death, is made a guilt offering, and bears the sin of many (Isaiah 53:10-12). Scholars debate how directly the wording draws on Isaiah 53, since Isaiah does not use the word ransom, but the idea of one life given in place of many is the heart of that chapter, and Matthew elsewhere reads Jesus' ministry through it: he quotes Isaiah 53:4 of Jesus' healings (8:17), and at the Last Supper Jesus calls the cup his blood of the covenant ‘poured out for many’, adding in Matthew alone ‘for the forgiveness of sins’ (26:28). The one who will sit on his glorious throne (19:28) must first drink the cup of suffering.

The request for the places at his right and left receives an answer Matthew makes visible at the cross. When Jesus is enthroned with the charge ‘This is Jesus, the King of the Jews’ over his head, two robbers are crucified with him, one on his right and one on his left (27:37-38), and the mother of the sons of Zebedee is among the women watching from a distance (27:56). The glory she asked for is revealed on a cross.

The parable shows who God is in Jesus' ministry. The owner who goes out again and again to find workers, who asks why they stand idle, and who gives the latecomers a full day's wage acts as Jesus acts toward tax collectors and sinners (9:10-13, 11:19, 21:31). The owner's question, ‘are you envious because I am generous?’ is the question Jesus puts to those who resent his welcome of the last.

Finally, the blind men call him ‘Lord, Son of David’ on the last stage of the road to David's city. Jesus stops, asks what they want, is moved with compassion, and touches them, and they follow him. The king who is about to be acclaimed in Jerusalem shows his royal power by serving the poorest, and those who see him rightly follow him to the cross.
interpretation:
The parable of the vineyard workers was read by the fathers as a story of God's calling through history. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 4.36.7) took the hours as the times in which one God called workers from the creation of the world to its end, answering those who divided the God of Israel from the Father of Jesus. Gregory the Great, preaching to catechumens in the basilica of Saint Lawrence in Rome in 591 (Homilies on the Gospels 19), gave a double reading that became standard in the Middle Ages: the hours are the ages of the world from Adam to Christ, and they are also the stages of a human life, from childhood to old age, so that no one should despair of being called late. John Chrysostom (Homily 64 on Matthew) warned that not every detail should be pressed, since there is no envy among the saints, and read the parable as encouragement to those who come to faith late in life. In the traditional Roman and Lutheran lectionaries the parable was the Gospel for Septuagesima, the third Sunday before Lent, and Johann Sebastian Bach's cantata Nimm, was dein ist, und gehe hin (BWV 144, first performed in Leipzig on 6 February 1724) sets verse 14 as its opening chorus. The Revised Common Lectionary reads it in September of Year A (Proper 20). Rembrandt's small panel of 1637, now in the Hermitage, sets the payment in a dim counting house with the grumbling workers pressing around the table.

The parable has had a long life in economic thought. John Ruskin took the title of his essays on political economy, Unto This Last (1860, as a book 1862), from the King James wording of verse 14, arguing for a just wage against the economics of his day; Mohandas Gandhi read it in 1904, called it the book that changed his life, and paraphrased it in Gujarati as Sarvodaya (1908). Modern scholars read the story in sharply different ways. Joachim Jeremias (The Parables of Jesus, German 1947) heard it as Jesus' defense of the good news to the poor against critics who resented his welcome of sinners. William Herzog (Parables as Subversive Speech, 1994) read the owner as an exploitative member of the elite who shames the workers when they protest. Amy-Jill Levine (Short Stories by Jesus, 2014) argues that Jesus' first hearers would have seen a landowner who hires everyone who needs work and pays each a living wage, a model for the rich rather than a symbol of God. A rabbinic parable in the Jerusalem Talmud (y. Berakhot 2:8), told at the funeral of Rabbi Bun bar Hiyya, who died young, describes a king who paid a worker hired for two hours a full day's wage because he accomplished more in two hours than the others in a day; comparing the two, many interpreters note that the rabbinic king rewards merit while Matthew's owner gives out of goodness.

Verse 28 anchored early reflection on the atonement. Origen, commenting on this verse (Commentary on Matthew 16.8), held that the ransom was paid to the devil, who held humanity captive; Gregory of Nazianzus (Oration 45.22) rejected payment to the evil one and denied that the Father demanded the price. Anselm's Why God Became Man (1098), the Reformers' teaching on substitution, and Gustaf Aulén's Christus Victor (English 1931) all claimed the verse. Verses 20 to 28 are the Gospel for the feast of Saint James on 25 July in the Roman calendar. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.65) explained Matthew's two blind men by suggesting that Bartimaeus was the better known of the two, which is why Mark names him and his father; he treated Luke's account as another healing. Nicolas Poussin's The Blind of Jericho (1650, now in the Louvre) follows Matthew, showing Christ touching the eyes of two men outside the city.
text:
English Bibles differ at several points in this chapter, mostly where the King James Version follows later manuscripts that filled out Matthew from other passages.

Verse 16: the KJV adds ‘for many be called, but few chosen’, a line found in many later manuscripts and taken from 22:14. It is absent from Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, and other early witnesses, and modern Bibles omit it. Verse 15: manuscripts differ over whether the owner's second question begins with ‘or’, a small difference of style. Verses 22 and 23: the KJV's ‘and to be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with’ comes from later manuscripts that borrowed it from Mark 10:38-39; the early manuscripts of Matthew mention only the cup.

Verse 28: Codex Bezae, the Old Latin, and the Curetonian Syriac add a long passage after this verse, telling the disciples to seek to rise from what is small rather than to be made less from what is great, and not to take the places of honor at a dinner lest someone more distinguished arrive and they be told to move down, a close relative of Luke 14:8-10. No modern Bible includes it, but it shows how the Western text sometimes expanded sayings.

Verses 30 and 31: manuscripts differ over the order and presence of ‘Lord’ and ‘Jesus’ in the blind men's cry, so that some Bibles read ‘Have mercy on us, O Lord, thou son of David’ (KJV) and others ‘Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us’ (BSB). The differences do not change the sense. Verse 17: some manuscripts read ‘the twelve disciples’ and others simply ‘the Twelve’.

teach.big: In the kingdom of heaven reward is grace, greatness is service, and the Son of Man gives his life as a ransom for many, so those who see him ask for mercy rather than thrones and follow him to the cross.

outline.t: God goes out again and again to call workers, even at the eleventh hour, and those no one else would hire are sent into his vineyard.
The owner pays everyone out of his goodness, not by the hour, and the grumbling of the first exposes the evil eye that resents grace given to others.
Jesus goes up to Jerusalem knowing he will be handed over, mocked, flogged, and crucified, and he promises that he will be raised on the third day.
Those who ask for glory must first share the cup, and places of honor belong to the Father's gift, not to family influence or ambition.
In Jesus' community greatness is service and the first place is the slave's, because the Son of Man came to serve and to give his life as a ransom in the place of many.
Two blind beggars see what the disciples have missed: they cry for mercy, the compassionate Son of David touches them, and they follow him.

teach.pitfalls:
The vineyard parable is often taught as if its only lesson were deathbed conversions, or as if it taught that all believers receive identical rewards in heaven; it is told to disciples who were calculating what they would receive (19:27), and its target is the envious eye that resents generosity. It is also misused as a charter for employers to ignore justice. The owner pays every worker at least a full day's wage, and the law he assumes required prompt payment; the parable does not teach that pay may be arbitrary, and readers such as Levine have noticed that it describes an employer who provides for all who need work.

The story of James and John's mother is often used to mock ambitious mothers or to single out the two brothers as villains; the ten were indignant because they wanted the same seats, and Matthew has Jesus answer the sons, not only the mother. Verse 28 should not be flattened into a lesson on servant leadership detached from the atonement, nor into a doctrine of the atonement detached from service; Jesus joins the two, and the servant pattern of leadership is grounded in the ransom. Avoid teaching verse 23 as if the brothers' request were simply refused: Jesus says the seats are the Father's to give. With the healing at Jericho, avoid either harmonizing the accounts so hard that each Gospel's own shape is lost or treating the differences as if they cancelled the event; teach Matthew's own emphasis on compassion, touch, and following.
teach.pastoral: The parable will press on people who feel they came late: those converted in old age, those who spent years away from God, those who have spent a lifetime serving and feel overlooked. It says the same thing to both, that the gift was never wages. It may also touch people who know the marketplace of day labor, unemployment, or being the one no one picks; the owner's question, ‘Why have you been standing here all day long doing nothing?’, meets the answer ‘Because no one has hired us’, and the story does not blame them. The request of James and John's mother may touch parents who carry ambition for their children, and the ten's indignation touches everyone who has resented another's advancement. Verse 28 may press on people who have been told to ‘serve’ in ways that excused others' abuse of power; Jesus' teaching condemns lording it over others and never requires a person to remain under mistreatment in the name of service.

hard.q: Isn't the landowner unfair to the workers who labored all day?
hard.a:
Most readers instinctively side with the first workers, and the objection has been put sharply. They worked twelve hours through the heat and received what the latecomers received for one. If pay is not proportioned to work, the parable seems to sanction arbitrary treatment, and if the owner stands for God, God seems arbitrary too. Social historians press a further point. William Herzog (Parables as Subversive Speech, 1994) argued that the owner is a wealthy landholder who exploits a surplus of desperate laborers, pays a bare subsistence wage, and then shames the one worker who dares to protest, so that reading him as God baptizes oppression. Others note that the owner's defense, ‘Do I not have the right to do as I please with what is mine?’, is the language of property, not of justice.

Responses begin with the story's own terms. The owner answers that he has done the first workers no wrong: they agreed to a denarius, a fair day's wage, and received it at the time the law required. Their complaint is not that they were cheated but that others were treated generously, and the owner names it as an evil eye. Joachim Jeremias (1947) read the parable in the setting of Jesus' ministry, where tax collectors and sinners entering the kingdom late offended those who had kept the law all their lives; many read it in Matthew's setting, after Peter's question in 19:27, as a warning to disciples not to think of the kingdom as a wage system in which those who give up more deserve more; others hear in it the admission of Gentiles alongside Jewish believers. Amy-Jill Levine (2014) answers Herzog from the other side, arguing that the owner who seeks out the unemployed and pays every one of them enough to live is precisely the kind of rich man the story commends. A rabbinic parable in the Jerusalem Talmud (y. Berakhot 2:8) has a king pay a worker hired late the full wage because he achieved more in two hours than others did all day; the comparison sharpens Matthew's point, since his owner gives the latecomers a full wage not for their productivity but because he is good. Christian readers have drawn from this the conviction that salvation is a gift equally given, not earned by length or quality of service, while disagreeing about whether the parable also teaches anything about rewards in heaven. The parable does not settle the social question the critics raise, but it asks every hearer whether they can rejoice when grace goes to someone else.

hard.q: Did Jesus heal two blind men leaving Jericho, as Matthew says, or one, as Mark and Luke say, and was he leaving the town or entering it?
hard.a:
The objection is a straightforward comparison. Mark 10:46-52 tells of one blind man, Bartimaeus, healed as Jesus was leaving Jericho; Luke 18:35-43 tells of one unnamed man healed as Jesus approached Jericho; Matthew tells of two men healed as Jesus and his disciples left the town. Critics since the eighteenth century have cited the passage as a clear contradiction among the Gospels, and many scholars who hold that Matthew used Mark see here a pattern of Matthew's editing: he doubles the Gadarene demoniac (8:28, compare Mark 5:2) and tells a similar story of two blind men earlier (9:27-31). Robert Gundry and others have suggested that Matthew doubled the figures to make up for stories of Mark's he left out, such as the blind man at Bethsaida (Mark 8:22-26); others suggest he wanted two witnesses, as the law required for testimony (Deuteronomy 19:15). On such views the number is Matthew's literary choice, not a historical report.

Harmonizers have offered several answers. Augustine (Harmony of the Gospels 2.65) argued that there were two men and that Mark and Luke name only the better known, Bartimaeus, whose father's name Mark also gives; mentioning one does not deny the other. For the location, some note that New Testament Jericho and the ruins of Old Testament Jericho lay about 2 kilometers apart, so that Jesus could be leaving one while approaching the other; others think the men first cried out as Jesus entered and were healed as he left, or that Luke placed the healing at the entrance because he goes on to tell of Zacchaeus in the town (Luke 19:1-10). Scholars who treat the differences as the ordinary variations of ancient narrative, such as Craig Keener and Michael Licona, argue that ancient biographers regularly compressed, relocated, and simplified details without being thought false. Christians who hold a high view of Scripture are found among both the harmonizers and those who see here Matthew's editorial freedom, and the core of the event is the same in all three Gospels: blind men on the road near Jericho cry to the Son of David for mercy, receive sight, and follow him toward Jerusalem.

observe: At what hours does the owner go out to hire workers, what does he promise each group, and in what order does he pay them?
What does the third passion prediction add to the earlier ones in 16:21 and 17:22-23?
Compare what the mother asks in verse 21 with what the blind men ask in verse 33. How does Jesus respond to each?
interpret: Why do the first workers grumble, and what does the owner mean by asking whether their eye is evil because he is good?
What do the cup and the right and left hand mean in verses 22 and 23, and how does the crucifixion scene in 27:37-38 cast light on them?
How does verse 28 explain both why Jesus' followers should serve and why Jesus must die?
apply: Which workers in the parable do you identify with most, and where do you find it hard to rejoice when grace goes to someone else?
Where in your family, church, or work are you seeking the seat at the right hand, and what would it look like to serve there instead?
If Jesus asked you, “What do you want Me to do for you?” what would you honestly say?
